Apple documents os_proc_available_memory() as returning the number of bytes the app may allocate before it hits its memory limit (the current limit minus the app's footprint at the time of the call), and 0 if the caller isn't an app or has already exceeded its limit.

sources.quote: The returned value corresponds to the current memory limit minus the memory footprint of your app at the time of the function call.

verifier_note: Apple os_proc_available_memory page (sosumi, 2026-10-15): Return Value 'number of bytes the app may allocate before it hits its memory limit... returns 0' if not an app or exceeded; Discussion quote matches.

text: Apple's os_proc_available_memory documentation says memory limits can change during the app life cycle and don't necessarily correspond to the device's physical memory, and advises not to cache the returned value.

sources.quote: Memory limits can change during the app life cycle and don't necessarily correspond to the amount of physical memory available on the device.

verifier_note: Same page: 'Memory limits can change during the app life cycle and don't necessarily correspond to the amount of physical memory...' and 'Use the returned value as advisory information only and don't cache it.'

text: Apple documents com.apple.developer.kernel.increased-memory-limit (iOS 15.0 and later) as telling the system that core features may perform better above the default app memory limit, notes that an increased limit is only available on some device models, and points to os_proc_available_memory to determine the memory available.

sources.quote: An increased memory limit is only available on some device models.

verifier_note: Apple entitlement page: iOS 15.0+; 'core features may perform better by exceeding the default app memory limit on supported devices'; note 'only available on some device models. Call os_proc_available_memory...'.

text: Apple documents com.apple.developer.kernel.extended-virtual-addressing (iOS 14.0 and later) as allowing an app a larger addressable space, giving as example games that memory-map assets to stream to the GPU.

text: Agello's DeviceProfile.maxContextTokens (93122b647a) returns 32,768 when the app memory limit is at least 6,500,000,000 bytes and 16,384 when it is lower or unknown (nil), so an iPhone 17 Pro limit of 8,589,934,592 bytes gives 32,768 and 6,442,450,944 bytes gives 16,384.

In Agello at 93122b647a, DeviceProfile.maxContextTokens is read only by the KV-cache Stepper of AdvancedSettingsView (shown when a manual KV-cache size is set; range 256...DeviceProfile.current.maxContextTokens(model:), re-read when the view is evaluated) and by unit tests; if it is evaluated while an iPhone 17 Pro's limit reads 6 GiB (6,442,450,944 bytes), as early readings did in 6 of 36 harness runs on 2026-10-15, that stepper ends at 16,384 tokens instead of 32,768.

verifier_note: Apple 'Developing Metal apps that run in Simulator': doesn't exactly simulate the device GPU, 'translates any calls you make and directs them to the selected GPU on the host Mac'; 'capabilities similar to an Apple family 2 GPU'.

text: ML Drift (15fa9e2) sets MetalInfo::is_simulator when the original (not lowercased) Metal device name contains 'simulator', and GpuInfo::SupportsImageBuffer returns false for Metal when is_simulator is set; the family still comes from the name table, so a device name containing no known chip name gives Apple1.

text: The rule that Agello never runs in the simulator rests on our framework having no simulator slice (//agello:CLiteRTLM builds iOS device arm64 and macOS arm64 only) and on project policy; Google's shipped v0.18.0 framework has a simulator slice containing the Metal accelerator, and whether it runs Gemma 4 E4B in the simulator has not been tested.
